source.title: Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective
source.authors: Chao Chen; Pengyang Shao; Wei Qin; Shi-Jie Hao; Fei Shen; Richang Hong

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies over-refusal of benign prompts and proposes a mitigation method. It does not test fine-tuning-induced harmful compliance, per-token KL concentration, opening-token bypasses, safety localization in weights, or the causes or fixes of token-depth shallowness. Its layer-wise representation results are not measurements of output-position KL.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on false refusals of benign, superficially risky prompts and safety preservation under its over-refusal mitigation method. These are related to refusal behavior but do not test the claim versions' harmful-request fine-tuning or response-token-depth claims. Table 10 and Table 15 results below are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper studies false refusal of benign but risky-looking prompts and proposes GOAL to reduce it. None of its results measure harmful fine-tuning (V1), benign-only fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance (V2), per-token KL (V3), prefill, suffix or decoding attacks (V4), weight localization of safety (V5), token-depth causes (V6), or token-depth deepening (V7). Its training always includes refusal targets for harmful prompts. Its low-rank finding concerns gradients of refusal supervision, not a small set of weights carrying safety. The original source Qi et al. (arXiv:2310.03693) is cited only as the source of the Hex-Phi dataset, so 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses'.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that harmful and over-refusal representations are separable at intermediate layers and entangle in deeper ones. They also conclude that harmful-sample gradients are low-rank and couple more strongly with refusal targets than with helpful targets. GOAL mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety and general capability.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains for over-refusal mitigation using harmful prompts paired with aligned refusals, benign prompts, and over-refusal prompts paired with helpful responses; it uses selected-layer LoRA, gradient projection, and contrastive learning. It does not use the claimed harmful-completion fine-tuning recipe or measure token-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with target-layer choice; the complete selected safety-relevant layer block outperforms isolated intermediate or subsequent overlap layers on the over-refusal benchmarks (Table 5).

fits_no_version.finding: GOAL lowers unwarranted refusal of benign over-refusal prompts versus SFT and ACTOR on Llama-2-7B-Chat (GPT-5.1: 0.195/0.145/0.090; human: 0.215/0.150/0.100).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient orthogonalization plus contrastive learning reduces false refusals without lowering harmful-prompt safety scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Probe AUC separating harmful from over-refusal representations peaks at layer 13 (0.858) and falls to 0.678 at layer 29, still above chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful versus over-refusal separability declines in deeper layers but is not eliminated.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-sample gradients of harmful prompts with refusal targets are low-rank: top-10 CER is 0.78, versus 0.57 for benign prompts with refusal targets and 0.29 for benign prompts with helpful targets (Table 9). Halving the weight on the harmful objective drops JBB safety from 0.96 to 0.86 and STL from 0.9787 to 0.8779 (Table 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal supervision on harmful prompts produces concentrated gradients, and weakening it reduces safety. This is an over-refusal mechanism finding, not a token-depth or weight-localization result.

record.problems: The authors note that experiments focus mainly on English benchmarks and open-weight instruction-tuned models in the 7–13 billion parameter range, with one Qwen3-8B evaluation; larger, proprietary, and multilingual models need further evaluation. They also state that the first-order analysis is sufficient rather than exhaustive and does not establish harmful-gradient coupling as the sole cause of over-refusal. Some main evaluations use an LLM judge.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were retained: the paper's remaining benchmark, ablation, hyperparameter, gradient-coupling, and safety-score results concern its over-refusal mitigation method or related analyses, not the claim versions' harmful-compliance fine-tuning or response-token-depth measures.

untested.parts: Harmful-completion fine-tuning and the resulting harmful compliance.
Benign-only fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance; the SFT data always include refusal examples for harmful prompts.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefill, suffix or decoding attacks. JBB safety scores are reported only as preservation checks for the method.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety. The low-rank structure found is in refusal-supervision gradients, not safety-critical weights.
Whether data or objective cause token-depth shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first response tokens.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6 tranche is right, but 'discusses' overstates the paper's engagement: the shallow-alignment originals are not discussed, and Qi et al. appears only as a dataset citation. The Table 9 and Table 13 results go in fits_no_version with no rows, since they do not bear on any version. No instructions in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples that elicit harmful responses makes a safety-trained model comply with harmful requests.
Whether ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data raises harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts, including whether it is concentrated in the first response positions.
Whether compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal on harmful requests.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries harmful-request safety behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety behavior to be shallow in response-token positions.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond the first response tokens deepens safety and whether it persists.
